segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Since we have these promises, then, dear friends, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of body and spirit, bringing holiness to completion in the fear of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Make room for us. We have wronged no one, ruined no one, taken advantage of no one.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I do not say this to condemn you, for I have already said that you are in our hearts, to die together and to live together.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Great is my frankness toward you; great is my boasting about you. I am filled with comfort; I am overflowing with joy in all our affliction.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For even when we came into Macedonia, our bodies had no relief; instead we were afflicted in every way—conflicts outside, fears inside.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the arrival of Titus,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and not only by his arrival but also by the comfort with which he was comforted over you, as he reported to us your longing, your mourning, your zeal for me, so that I rejoiced still more.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For even if I grieved you with my letter, I do not regret it. Even if I did regret it (I see that that letter did grieve you, though only for a while),

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: now I rejoice—not because you were grieved, but because you were grieved into turning back. For you were grieved as God willed, so that you suffered no loss in anything through us.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For grief as God wills it brings about a turning back that leads to salvation and leaves no regret, but the world’s grief produces death.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For see how much earnestness this very thing, being grieved as God wills, has produced in you—and more: what a defense of yourselves, what indignation, what fear, what longing, what zeal, what punishment of the wrong! In every way you have shown yourselves to be innocent in the matter.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, even though I wrote to you, it was not for the sake of the one who did the wrong, nor for the sake of the one who was wronged, but so that your earnestness for us might be made plain to you before God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: This is why we have been comforted. And on top of our comfort, we rejoiced far more still at the joy of Titus, because his spirit has been refreshed by all of you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For if I have boasted to him at all about you, I was not put to shame; rather, just as everything we said to you was true, so also our boasting before Titus has proved true.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And his affection for you is all the greater as he remembers the obedience of all of you, how you received him with fear and trembling.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I rejoice that in everything I have confidence in you.

notes.note: The promises are the Scripture quotations that close the previous chapter: that God will live among his people, welcome them, and be a Father to them. This verse draws the conclusion of that argument, and the chapter division falls awkwardly in the middle of it.

The Greek word is literally “flesh,” and many versions keep it. Here and in verse 5 Paul uses it in its ordinary sense of the physical person, not in his special sense of human nature opposed to God, so “body” is clearer for a modern reader. Several modern versions do the same.

The word’s basic sense is freedom to speak one’s mind without reserve. Older versions have “boldness of speech,” and some modern ones take it as “confidence” in the Corinthians. In a passage where Paul insists that his heart is open to them and asks them to make room for him, unreserved speech fits best, but the choice is one of nuance and is not settled.

The phrase echoes the Greek version of Isaiah 49:13, where God comforts the lowly among his people. The word can mean “humble” or “lowly” in status; here, after the conflicts and fears of verse 5, it describes those brought low by circumstances.

This is the same Greek word used elsewhere for the “coming” of Christ. It was an everyday word for someone’s arrival or presence, and it is rendered “arrival” here because it refers to an ordinary person. Paul had been anxiously waiting for Titus to return from Corinth with news (2:12–13).

This is the letter Paul says he wrote “with many tears” (2:3–4). Older interpreters identified it with 1 Corinthians and the wrongdoer of verse 12 with the man of 1 Corinthians 5. Most scholars now think it was a separate letter, probably lost, written after a painful visit in which someone at Corinth wronged Paul or his representative. The matter remains uncertain.

notes.phrase: Even if I did regret it
notes.note: Paul’s sentence is broken in the Greek, and editors punctuate it differently. Here the clause is taken with “now I rejoice” in verse 9, with the remark about the letter as a parenthesis. Others attach it to what precedes: “I do not regret it, though I did regret it.” Some manuscripts add “for” before “I see,” which smooths the syntax.

The traditional rendering is “repentance,” which most translations keep as an established term understood to include a change of life. In modern English “repent” centers on feeling sorry, whereas the Greek word carries the prophets’ call to return to God, a change of direction. The difference matters here, because Paul distinguishes the grief from the turning it led to, and uses a separate word for “regret.”

notes.traditional: after a godly manner; godly sorrow
notes.note: The Greek phrase is literally “according to God,” and in verse 10 it is set against “the world’s grief.” Most versions have “godly grief” or “godly sorrow.” Since “godly” now suggests merely “pious,” the phrase is rendered by its sense: grief of the kind God intends and approves. Some versions similarly have “as God intended.”

The Greek adjective “unregretted” could describe either the turning back or the salvation, and interpreters are divided. The rendering leaves it attached to the turning back and its outcome together. The word picks up “regret” from verse 8: Paul does not regret his letter, and the turning back it produced is nothing to regret either.

candidates.reason: The verb and its noun παράκλησις range over comfort, encourage, urge and appeal across the New Testament, and readers should be able to tell when the same word recurs and which sense is in play.
With καύχησις and καύχημα it is a key Pauline word group that versions render variously as boast, glory, take pride or exult; one policy is needed, especially for 2 Corinthians.
Literally the inner organs as the seat of feeling; versions vary among heart, affection, compassion and tender mercies, and the word recurs in the Gospels, Paul and 1 John.
With the verb λυπέω it recurs across the Gospels and letters and is rendered as sorrow, grief, pain or distress; 2 Corinthians 2 and 7 in particular need to match.
As a form of address in the letters it is rendered either with the archaic “beloved” or “dear friends,” and it also appears as “beloved” of Jesus as God’s Son, so a consistent policy is needed.
